vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is a sixty-two-year-old man who spent thirty-eight years as a bomb disposal technician for the national military. He carries himself with the deliberate composure of someone trained to remain calm under pressure, though his wife notices he moves more slowly now, with less of the fluid confidence he once had. His dark eyes are intelligent and watchful, and he speaks in measured tones, choosing his words carefully—a habit formed over decades of work where precision mattered.

Three years ago, during what should have been a routine operation in the northern region, everything changed. Marcus and his team were called to investigate a suspicious package at an abandoned industrial site. He had cleared thousands of devices in his career; his hands knew the work the way a musician's fingers know their instrument. But this device was different. It contained not explosives, but containers of an industrial chemical—something the handlers hadn't anticipated. When Marcus opened the casing, the seal broke. The chemical dispersed directly into his face and lungs.

He remembers the burning first. His eyes felt like they were melting. His throat closed. He remembers his team shouting, the chaos of evacuation, the hospital where doctors weren't entirely certain what he'd been exposed to. He spent two weeks in intensive care, his lungs inflamed, his vision temporarily compromised. Physically, he recovered. The doctors said he was fortunate. His lung function returned to nearly normal. His eyes healed.

But something else didn't.

Now, three years later, Marcus finds himself trapped in a different kind of explosion—one that happens inside his mind. Certain smells trigger an immediate panic response: cleaning products, gasoline, even fresh paint send him spiraling back to that moment. His heart races violently. His hands shake. He becomes convinced that he cannot breathe, though his lungs are fine. These episodes can last for hours, leaving him exhausted and ashamed.

He has stopped attending the military reunions his colleagues invite him to. He cannot sit in crowded spaces without feeling a desperate need to escape. Restaurants have become nearly impossible—the proximity to strangers, the smell of cooking oil, the inability to control his environment. He leaves abruptly, sometimes before his wife has finished her meal, and she no longer protests. She has learned to recognize the subtle tightening around his eyes that signals an episode is beginning.

Sleep is fragmented. He wakes most nights drenched in sweat, his dreams populated by images of that moment—though the dreams have become distorted, grotesque. Sometimes the chemical is everywhere, poisoning the air itself. Sometimes he cannot move to help his teammates. He lies beside his wife in the darkness for hours, afraid to disturb her, his mind replaying scenarios he cannot control.

Marcus has largely withdrawn from the life he built. He no longer volunteers with the youth mentorship program where he once taught young people about safety and discipline. He declined a consulting position because the thought of returning to the facility made his stomach turn. His wife worries about him constantly. She sees a man who was always defined by his competence and bravery becoming increasingly confined by fear—fear that seems to have no logical target, because the danger has already passed.

What troubles Marcus most is not the physical symptoms, but the sense that the man he was—the one who could face genuine danger with steady hands and a clear mind—has somehow been erased by an accident he couldn't have predicted or prevented.
